topic: QT prolongation and cardiac safety during drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment

key_clinical_concepts.preferred_correction: QTcF (Fridericia), particularly in TB drug-safety monitoring
key_clinical_concepts.prolonged: WHO guidance cited in this repository considers QTcF >450 ms prolonged.
key_clinical_concepts.high_risk_threshold: QTcF >=500 ms is associated with increased risk of potentially life-threatening arrhythmia.

monitoring.who_general_ecg_schedule: Ideally baseline, week 2, week 4, then every 4 weeks while receiving combinations of QT-prolonging TB drugs, plus additional ECGs when clinically indicated.
monitoring.bedaquiline_product_info: ECG before treatment and at least monthly; correct potassium, calcium and magnesium abnormalities before treatment and monitor electrolytes if QT is prolonged.
monitoring.symptom_trigger: If syncope occurs, obtain ECG and urgent clinical assessment.

interaction_logic: QT-prolonging effects can be additive when bedaquiline is combined with clofazimine, delamanid, moxifloxacin or other QT-prolonging medicines.
Do not classify a combination as contraindicated solely because two QT-prolonging drugs are present; current DR-TB regimens may intentionally combine them with monitoring.
Review non-TB QT-prolonging medicines and avoid unnecessary combinations when possible.
Correct potassium, magnesium and calcium abnormalities and evaluate other reversible causes.
safety_rules: Do not diagnose clinically significant QT prolongation from palpitations alone; retrieve ECG/QTcF.
Syncope or near-syncope during a QT-prolonging regimen is a high-priority symptom.
QTcF >=500 ms requires prompt clinician-led review of QT-prolonging drugs and reversible causes; do not instruct the patient to independently restart therapy.
Differentiate mild/asymptomatic QT changes from ventricular arrhythmia or syncope.
Do not use Bazett-corrected QT interchangeably with QTcF when applying WHO QTcF thresholds.
Medication changes must follow the current regimen-specific guideline and treating team.
